title: Deep learning for structural health monitoring
intro: Detecting subtle changes in ultrasonic signals while accounting for variation in environmental and operating conditions.
summary: Guided-wave signals change with both structural condition and the environment. I developed an LSTM model trained on healthy ultrasonic data, using deviations from predicted healthy responses to identify synthetic defect signals. Healthy-only training avoids requiring damaged examples during model training.
role: I led a five-person undergraduate team, organising meetings, coordinating milestones and integrating individual contributions. I personally developed the LSTM model in Python/PyTorch, then independently extended the research over summer and benchmarked it against a multistep NARX baseline from the published literature.
decisions: Train on healthy data to learn normal signal behaviour before evaluating synthetic defects.
Compare models across defect amplitudes and arrival times, rather than relying on a single favourable condition.
Use ROC-AUC to assess how effectively anomaly scores distinguish healthy and defective signals.
results: At −40 dB, mean ROC-AUC was 0.991 for the LSTM and 0.744 for NARX. At −45 dB, it was 0.814 versus 0.511. Both models reached 1.000 at −30 dB and −35 dB in the reported evaluation.
limits: Results are for synthetic defect signals across the evaluated arrival times. ROC-AUC measures discrimination, not percentage accuracy. These results do not establish performance on every physical defect or operating condition.

report_note: This report documents the original team project comparing LSTM, CNN and optimal baseline subtraction. The NARX comparison shown above comes from the subsequent summer extension and is not presented as a result from this report.

title: Deployable vehicle-mounted solar array
alt: CAD assembly of the deployed solar array
intro: A compact roof-mounted array designed to expand its collection area when a camper is parked.
summary: Our team developed a deployable solar array for UK campers. Consumer research and environmental studies informed a quantified product design specification. We explored concepts through rapid linkage prototypes and a weighted trade-off matrix, then developed CAD and assessed the proposed system’s feasibility.
role: My contributions covered consumer research, the product design specification, concept generation, linkage prototyping, CAD iterations and material selection. I also designed a compound gearbox using catalogue gears to meet the target velocity ratio.
decisions: Translate user needs into measurable requirements for deployment, mass and packaging.
Compare linkage concepts before committing to the final arrangement.
Use catalogue gear selection and modelling to develop the compound gearbox.
Assess the energy benefit alongside added drag, system mass and cost.
results: The design exceeded its 2:1 area-expansion target. Calculated deployment time was below the 25-second requirement and estimated mass was below the 80 kg limit. The seven-day peak-condition scenario compared 339.6 Wh of drag energy with up to 3,080 Wh of potential generation.
limits: These are design calculations and feasibility estimates, not measured full-system prototype performance. Energy generation depends on the scenario and conditions.
images: Linkage geometry in the deployed and retracted positions.
Motor efficiency curves used in component assessment.
report_note: Group coursework reports by Ka Hin Cheung, Ethan Smith, James Matteucci and Alex Winter. My individual contribution is described above.

title: Structural analysis of a lifting lug
alt: Abaqus stress contour of a lifting lug
intro: Linking finite-element analysis, fracture mechanics and inspection planning for a pressure-vessel lifting attachment.
summary: I analysed a welded lifting lug for a 12,000 kg pressure vessel. The work combined a hand-derived quadratic triangular element, an energy-consistency check and a three-dimensional Abaqus model using quadratic tetrahedral elements.
role: I carried out the structural analysis, assessed mesh convergence and interpreted stresses near singularity-dominated regions. I then examined strain-gauge warning thresholds and used fracture mechanics and Paris’ law to estimate an inspection interval.
decisions: Check the analytical element’s energy consistency before interpreting its stress predictions.
Use mesh refinement and stress averaging to assess numerical sensitivity.
Distinguish local singularity effects from stress measures useful for engineering assessment.
Relate crack growth and detection assumptions to an inspection interval.
results: The reported model gave a weld-line von Mises stress of 113.4 MPa and peak displacement of 24.42 µm. Fracture analysis gave a critical crack length of approximately 7.92 mm and an inspection interval of approximately 24,000 lifting cycles under the coursework assumptions.
limits: Mesh convergence is numerical verification rather than experimental validation. The 99% probability-of-detection assumption applies to the specified detectable crack size, not a blanket confidence level for the entire inspection recommendation.
images: Lug geometry and analytical element definition.
Mesh refinement study for the selected stress measure.

title: Thermal comfort in a camping tent
alt: Annotated heat-transfer diagram for a tent in hot conditions
intro: Using an energy balance to assess summer daytime overheating and cold-night heat loss.
summary: I modelled a simplified tent and its occupants using weather data, heat-transfer correlations and dimensionless analysis. The assessment considered convection, radiation and ground conduction for hot daytime and cold nighttime conditions.
role: I developed the thermal assessment and used it to propose ventilation and insulation changes for an outdoor-equipment design brief.
decisions: Separate hot and cold scenarios because their dominant heat-transfer mechanisms and design responses differ.
Compare predicted occupant heat storage with the coursework comfort criterion.
Assess increased ventilation for the hot case and a low-emissivity liner for the cold case.
results: Under the assumed airflow change, side vents increased calculated convective cooling from 18.9 to 34.3 W/m². The 15.4 W/m² increase exceeded the 14.3 W/m² reduction required in the hot-case model. A reflective liner was proposed to reduce radiative heat loss in the cold scenario.
limits: These are simplified model predictions. Interpretation depends on environmental conditions, airflow, exposed area and occupant/clothing assumptions; the proposed modifications were not experimentally validated in this assessment.
